title: Production handoff for LLM features - brief
content:
Purpose:
This one-pager frames Redwood’s core positioning for the specific buyer moment we call the "production handoff" — when product, ML, and platform teams need to move an LLM feature from prototype to reliable, cost-effective production. The doc is aimed at engineering leaders and platform/product cross-functional owners who own SLA, cost, and performance tradeoffs.

Top-line message:
Redwood removes the last-mile operational friction of shipping LLM-driven features: we make latency predictable, cost measurable, and rollouts safe so engineering teams can hand off prototypes and retain velocity without building a bespoke infra stack.

Why this matters now:
- Rapid prototyping has lowered the bar to build LLM features, but production is where complexity explodes (tail latency, cache management, throughput bursts, model regressions).
- Teams stall at the handoff: they either overprovision (cost) or under-engineer (reliability). Both harm product adoption.
- Buyers are pragmatic — they want to ship features that meet SLA and cost targets, not research wins.

Redwood thesis for the handoff:
- Handoff is primarily an operational problem, not a modeling problem. The differentiator is who can make serving predictable without sacrificing developer agility.
- The right product abstracts serving complexity (routing, batching, KV caching, graceful degradation) while surfacing economics and quality telemetry back to teams.

Core positioning pillars (3 lines):
1) Predictable Latency for UX: standard SLOs, adaptive routing, and fallback variants so product teams can design experiences with known response envelopes.
2) Accountable Economics: token-level cost attribution, autoscaling policies tuned to real traffic patterns, and quantization guidance to meet cost targets.
3) Safe Rollouts & Observability: per-prompt quality monitoring, canary A/B paths, and automatic fallback policies to prevent regressions in production.

What to say to engineering buyers (copy snippets):
- Elevator: "Ship the LLM feature. Keep the mops. Redwood makes production predictable — latency, cost, and availability — so your product team can iterate without guessing about infrastructure."
- 30s pitch: "You’ve proven the model works in lab. Redwood handles the serving complexity — from batching and KV caching to fallback models and cost telemetry — so you meet SLAs, control spend, and keep ownership of product decisions."

Proof points / signals of credibility (short):
- Real customers: replaced ad-hoc GPU pools and reduced 95th percentile latency by X-40% while lowering per-token cost by ~25% through caching and optimized batching.
- Platform design: single API for hosted/dedicated/private so integrations work across deployment modes.
- Operational features: token-level cost dashboards, rollout controls, and auditing hooks for compliance.

Competitive contrast (how to differentiate):
- Generic cloud endpoints: provide capacity but leave engineering teams to design batching, cache, and model-fallback strategies (higher dev time + unpredictable cost).
- Model-first vendors: strong model capabilities but weak operational tooling and no cross-environment deployment parity.
- Open-source runtimes: flexible but require significant ops and tuning to meet production SLOs and cost targets.

Objection handling (concise):
- "We can build this ourselves": Building predictable serving is a multi-quarter investment and becomes ongoing toil — Redwood accelerates time-to-stable-production and surfaces the economics so you don’t guess on capacity.
- "We need on-prem / VPC": Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem packages with the same API and rollout controls as hosted, minimizing rework.
- "We can use cloud autoscaling": Autoscaling raw capacity doesn’t solve batching inefficiencies, cache reuse, or regression detection — those are product-level controls Redwood provides.

Suggested GTM hooks (how to use this doc):
- Sales: use in discovery slides when a buyer says "we have a working prototype but are worried about scale/latency/cost".
- Solutions engineering: checklist for handoff intake (SLO targets, cost envelope, data residency, rollback plan, sample traffic shape).
- Marketing: short landing copy focused on "stop guessing about production" and a 3-step flow: prototype -> handoff -> live with SLA.

Intake checklist for PD/ML teams handing off to Redwood (operational questions to capture):
- Target p50/p95/p99 latency and budget per 1000 users.
- Expected QPS pattern (burstiness, diurnal, long-tail).
- Privacy/compliance requirements (regions, KMS).
- Acceptance criteria for quality (prompt sets and evaluation thresholds).
- Rollback/fallback policy requirements.

Next tactical steps (recommended playbook):
1) Run a 2-week pilot: connect prototype, capture traffic, and validate p95 with Redwood’s adaptive batching.
2) Define SLO + cost envelope and run a canary (1% traffic) with automatic fallback configured.
3) Iterate on quantization/batching settings informed by Redwood Optimize recommendations and verify quality on the accepted prompt set.

Appendix: sample positioning language for one-pager headline and subhead:
- Headline: "Turn prototypes into predictable products"
- Subhead: "Redwood handles serving complexity — low latency, clear economics, and safe rollouts — so engineering teams can ship LLM features that users rely on."

Notes for messaging nuance:
- Avoid research-centric words (e.g., "state-of-the-art") in this buyer moment; buyers here care about repeatability and risk reduction.
- Use measurable outcomes (latency percentiles, cost delta, time-to-production) to swap debate from features to economics.
- Provide a handoff checklist in all sales kits to make the transition tangible.

Document history and authorship:
